name: Reading Rail
summary: A table of contents that tracks reading position using a reading line rather than visibility, so the marker never flickers between two headings at a boundary.

attempts.prompt: Build a table of contents that highlights the current section as you scroll.
attempts.problem: Used IntersectionObserver and marked whichever heading was intersecting, so while two headings were on screen the highlight flickered between them on every scroll frame, and when a long section filled the viewport with no heading visible at all the highlight vanished entirely.

attempts.prompt: Stop the flicker and keep a section highlighted through long passages.
attempts.problem: Switched to the topmost visible heading, which stopped the vanishing but not the flicker: a heading straddling the top of the viewport enters and leaves repeatedly during ordinary scrolling. It also never marked the final section, because the last heading can sit above the viewport top once the reader reaches the end of the document.

finalPrompt:
Build a reading-position table of contents in plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, no dependencies, for a scrollable article region.

Do not decide the current section from visibility. Define a reading line at roughly 28 percent down the scroll container, and mark the last heading whose top has passed that line. Visibility-based approaches flicker whenever a heading straddles a boundary, and fail entirely when a long section fills the viewport with no heading in sight.

Handle the end explicitly: when the container is scrolled to the bottom, the final section is current even if its heading sits above the reading line. Without that, the last entry in the contents can never be reached, which is the bug every implementation of this has.

Draw the marker as a single element whose offset and height animate to the active link, rather than a class applied to each link. One travelling marker reads as position; per-link highlighting reads as selection.

Throttle the scroll handler through requestAnimationFrame and register it passive.

Mark the active link with aria-current and update it only when the index actually changes, so assistive technology is not told about every scroll frame.

Clicking a link scrolls the container, not the page, with smooth behaviour, and headings carry scroll-margin so they do not land flush against the top edge.

Recompute on resize, since the reading line and every offset depend on the container height.

Below about 520px, stack the contents above the article and drop the sticky positioning.

Colour comes only from CSS custom properties: var(--border), var(--text), var(--text-dim), var(--accent). No literal hex, rgb or hsl values.
why:
This is a component where the obvious tool is the wrong one. IntersectionObserver is what everyone reaches for, and it answers a question — is this element visible — that is not the question being asked. The question is where is the reader, and a reading line answers it directly and cannot flicker, because a heading's top passes a fixed line exactly once.

Stating that as the rule, rather than asking to fix the flicker, is what replaced the approach instead of patching it. A patch to a visibility-based implementation is always another special case.

The end-of-document case is worth remembering independently: any scroll-position mapping has a range at the bottom that no element's position can reach, so the final item needs an explicit rule. Nearly every scroll-spy in the wild has this bug.
